# @zireal/result-kit — full agent reference

> Type-safe `Result` handling for TypeScript. A plain, method-less `Result` union,
> a data-first free-function core, and an opt-in fluent wrapper. Zero runtime
> dependencies and no *required* peer dependencies (`vitest` is an **optional**
> peer, used only by the `/testing` subpath). ESM-only, Node >=22.12,
> TypeScript >=6.0. Current version: 5.x.

This is the long form of `llms.txt`. It is self-contained: everything an agent
needs to write, review, or migrate `@zireal/result-kit` code, including the
rationale behind the decisions that look surprising. Read `llms.txt` alone if you
only need to write correct code; read this when you need to know *why*, or when
you are doing something beyond the common path.

Contents:

1. Reflexes to unlearn (read first if you know neverthrow)
2. The union, and why it is plain data
3. Root API — the complete surface
4. Typed errors
5. Dispatching on the error — `matchType`
6. The two surfaces — core vs `/fluent`
7. Async
8. Do-notation — `safeTry`
9. Across the wire
10. Validation — `fromSchema`
11. Testing
12. Recipes
13. Gotchas, in full
14. Migrating from 1.x
15. Vocabulary

---

## 1. Reflexes to unlearn

An LLM writing for this package from prior training will produce `neverthrow`
idioms. They are close enough to look right and different enough not to compile.
Left column is the reflex; right column is what this package actually exports.

| Common reflex | Correct here | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `result.unwrapOr(0)` | `unwrapOr(result, 0)` | The core is **free functions**. Methods exist only on `/fluent` wrappers. |
| `result.map(f)` | `map(result, f)` | Data-first: the value is the first argument. |
| `result.andThen(f)` | `andThen(result, f)` | Same. |
| `result.match(okFn, errFn)` | `match(result, { ok, err })` | Ours takes **one object**, not two positional callbacks. This is the single most common miscompile. |
| `Result.combine([a, b])` | `combine([a, b])` | No static namespace object. And ours is **tuple-preserving**. |
| `Result.combineWithAllErrors([…])` | `combineWithAllErrors([…])` | Free function. |
| `result._unsafeUnwrap()` | `unwrapOrThrow(result)` | `_unsafeUnwrap` does not exist. `unwrapOrThrow` throws a real `Error` with the original in `cause`. |
| `result._unsafeUnwrapErr()` | `expectErr(result)` (tests only) | No production equivalent by design — narrow with `isErr`. |
| `okAsync(v)` / `errAsync(e)` | *(no equivalent)* | Async is `Promise<Result>` in the core, or `ResultAsync.from(...)` on `/fluent`. |
| `ResultAsync.fromPromise(p, fn)` | `fromPromise(p, fn)` | A free function, at the root **and** on `/fluent`. |
| `ResultAsync.fromSafePromise(p)` | *(no equivalent)* | Use `fromPromise` and supply the reject mapper. |
| `result.asyncMap(f)` | `.toAsync().map(f)` | Crossing sync→async is one explicit seam, not per-method twins. |
| `result.asyncAndThen(f)` | `.toAsync().andThen(f)` | Same. |
| `Result.fromThrowable(fn, onErr)` | `fromThrowable(fn, onErr)` | Free function. |
| `fromAsyncThrowable(fn, onErr)` | `fromThrowableAsync(fn, onErr)` | The `Async` suffix goes **last**, consistently. |
| `yield* mightFail()` (neverthrow 8.1+) | `yield* safeUnwrap(mightFail())` | **The dangerous one.** neverthrow's `Result` became directly iterable in 8.1.0; ours is deliberately **not**, so this looks like it should work. `safeUnwrap` is a free function, root-only. |
| `yield* mightFail().safeUnwrap()` (≤8.0) | `yield* safeUnwrap(mightFail())` | Same target. Still present in neverthrow 8.x — deprecated in 8.1.1, slated for removal in 9.0.0. |
| `err._tag` / `err.code` / `err.kind` | `err.type` | The discriminant is `type`. Always. |
| `Data.TaggedError` / `class E extends Error` | `defineError('not_found', …)` | Typed errors are **plain objects**, never classes. |
| `Option` / `Maybe` / `Some` / `None` | *(not shipped)* | Deliberately out of scope. Use `toNullable` / `fromNullable`. |
| `E.right(v)` / `E.left(e)` (fp-ts) | `ok(v)` / `err(e)` | |
| `pipe(x, E.map(f))` | `map(x, f)` or `/fluent` | No `pipe` ships. See §12. |
| `import from '@zireal/result-kit/core'` | `from '@zireal/result-kit'` | There is no `/core` subpath. The root **is** the core. |

### The one that bites hardest

**`neverthrow`'s `.isOk()` narrows. `/fluent`'s `.isOk()` does not.**

```ts
// ✗ WRONG — does not narrow, and `.value` does not exist on the wrapper
const chain = from(findUser(id));
if (chain.isOk()) chain.value;

// ✓ Leave the wrapper, then narrow with the free-function guard
const result = from(findUser(id)).toResult();
if (isOk(result)) result.value;   // T

// ✓ Or never leave — collapse both branches instead
from(findUser(id)).match({ ok: (u) => u.name, err: () => 'anonymous' });
```

`/fluent`'s `.isOk()` / `.isErr()` return **plain booleans** and buy no narrowing:
a method cannot emit a type predicate about its own class's generics. The root's
`isOk(r)` / `isErr(r)` *are* type predicates and do narrow.

`ResultAsync` does not have `.isOk()` / `.isErr()` **at all** — an always-truthy
`if (ra.isOk())` on a promise-like is a footgun, and narrowing needs the plain
union anyway.

---

## 2. The union, and why it is plain data

```ts
type Result<T, E> = Ok<T> | Err<E>;

interface Ok<T>  { readonly ok: true;  readonly value: T }
interface Err<E> { readonly ok: false; readonly error: E }
```

**Purely structural — there is no brand.** Any `{ ok: true, value }` *is* an
`Ok<T>`, whoever built it. Any `{ ok: false, error }` *is* an `Err<E>`.

The contract, in full:

- No class, no methods, no hidden brand, no `Symbol` tag.
- **Exactly two fields** per half. No opposite-field `never`, no third field.
- Shallow `readonly` only. No runtime `Object.freeze`.
- Not iterable. (Iterability lives on `safeUnwrap` and the `/fluent` wrappers.)

Each of those is load-bearing for one guarantee: a `Result` round-trips through
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` when `T` and `E` are JSON-serializable, and
arrives on the far side **still a usable `Result`** — no re-wrapping, no revival
step, no `instanceof` to fail.

```ts
const parsed = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(result)); // still a usable Result
```

That is the difference from every class-based library in the genre. A thrown
`Error` does not serialize (`JSON.stringify(new Error('x'))` is `{}`), and a
`Result` that is a class instance does not either — the methods are gone,
`instanceof` is false, and what arrives is a bag of fields wearing the wrong type.

**Three carve-outs**, and they are the only three:

1. **`cause` may hold anything.** It is the one field typed `unknown`, so it is
   the one route a non-serializable value takes in. Strip it at the boundary.
2. **Exit the wrapper first.** Serialize `chain.toResult()`, never the chain.
3. **`ok()` with no argument** round-trips to a one-field object — see §13.

Practical consequences when writing code:

- There is no `instanceof Result`. Use `isOk` / `isErr` / `isResult`.
- Do not add a `status`, a `timestamp`, or any third field to a `Result`.
- Do not add a top-level field to a `TypedError` either — nest it under `details`.

---

## 3. Root API — the complete surface

`@zireal/result-kit` exports **37 values and 14 types** from one flat barrel.
Import only what you use; the package is `sideEffects: false` and genuinely
tree-shakable — import three functions and ship three functions.

### Constructors and guards

```ts
ok(value)              // Ok<T>
ok()                   // Ok<void> — the no-arg overload, for Result<void, E>
err(error)             // Err<E> — the single generic failure constructor
isOk(r) / isErr(r)     // type predicates: `r is Ok<T>` / `r is Err<E>`
isTypedError(e)        // does this value follow the TypedError convention?
defineError(type, msg) // build a typed-error constructor
defineErrors(registry) // group constructors so ErrorsOf can derive the union
isResult(v)            // is this `unknown` a Result? (type predicate)
parseResult(v)         // the same check, with a typed error saying why it failed
```

There is **no** separate typed `fail` constructor. `err` takes any `E`, including
a `TypedError`.

### Transforms

Each accepts a `Result` **or** a `Promise<Result>` in the same signature — there
is no `Async`-suffixed twin of any of them.

```ts
map(r, fn)             // transform the value; Err passes through untouched
mapErr(r, fn)          // transform the error; Ok passes through untouched
andThen(r, fn)         // chain a fallible step; error channel widens to E | F
orElse(r, fn)          // recover from an error
inspect(r, fn)         // tee the Ok side for a side effect; returns r unchanged
inspectErr(r, fn)      // tee the Err side for a side effect
```

`andThen` **accumulates** the error channel — `Result<T, E>` plus a callback
returning `Result<U, F>` gives `Result<U, E | F>`. That is the same rule
do-notation uses. There is no Rust-style `From` coercion.

### Terminals

These leave the `Result` world.

```ts
match(r, { ok, err })  // collapse both branches to one value; exhaustive
unwrapOr(r, fallback)  // the value, or a fallback
unwrapOrElse(r, fn)    // the value, or a fallback computed from the error
unwrapOrThrow(r, msg?) // the value, or THROW a real Error (original in `cause`)
toNullable(r)          // the value, or null
```

`match`'s cases object is keyed `ok` / `err`. Both keys are required —
exhaustiveness is structural, not checked by a helper.

### Collections

```ts
combine(results)               // all-or-nothing; PRESERVES THE TUPLE TYPE; first Err wins
combineWithAllErrors(results)  // same success typing, but collects EVERY error into an array
partition(results)             // [values, errors] — both halves, always
```

```ts
combine([ok(1), ok('a')]);   // Result<[number, string], never> — a tuple, not (number|string)[]
```

`combineWithAllErrors` is the motivating source for `groupByType` and
`prettifyErrors`. `partition`'s second half is an equally valid input to both.

#### The record ("object form") overload

Both combinators also accept a **record** and return one keyed identically.
`partition` does **not** — record support is a property of the combinators, not
of the section. The array signatures are unchanged: an array of `Result`s is not
assignable to `Record<string, Result<unknown, unknown>>`, so the record overload
is unreachable for an array input and tuple preservation cannot degrade.

```ts
const combined = combine({ user: findUser(id), posts: listPosts(id) });
if (combined.ok) {
  const { user, posts } = combined.value;  // names survive; order does not matter
}
```

The record form of `combineWithAllErrors` accumulates `KeyedError<K, E>` entries
— `{ readonly key: K; readonly error: E }` — instead of a flat array. The pair is
**knowingly asymmetric**: a record knows the name of each part, and throwing that
away is the only reason not to pass one. The array form stays flat.

```ts
const checked = combineWithAllErrors({ name: checkName(i), age: checkAge(i) });
if (!checked.ok) {
  for (const entry of checked.error) {
    switch (entry.key) {
      case 'name': /* entry.error narrows to checkName's error type */ break;
      case 'age':  /* ...and to checkAge's here */ break;
    }
  }
}
```

**The bridge, and it is the one real cost.** `groupByType` and `prettifyErrors`
take a flat `TypedError[]`, and a `KeyedError[]` is not one:

```ts
prettifyErrors(checked.error.map((e) => e.error));
```

Four more facts, each decided rather than incidental:

- **"First Err" means property order, not order as written.**
  `combine({ 10: late, 2: early })` returns `early` — `Object.keys` yields
  integer-like keys in ascending numeric order *before* insertion-ordered string
  keys. `combineWithAllErrors` accumulates in that same order. Only own
  enumerable properties participate.
- **Symbol keys are silently invisible.** A symbol-keyed `Err` does not join the
  string index signature, so it type-checks and is dropped. Documented rather
  than closed: it matches the §2.1 serialization boundary.
- **`combine({})` is `ok({})`** — the empty-input identity in record form. An
  empty *array* still picks the array overload, so the two never contend.
- **A value in the bag that is not a `Result` throws a named diagnostic**, e.g.
  `combine: value at key "posts" is not a Result (received: undefined)`. An
  optional key may carry `undefined` as a *present* own key. It stays a hard
  failure — a non-`Result` in the bag is a programming error — but it names the
  key instead of throwing a bare `TypeError`. The array path takes the same
  guard, since a hole in a sparse array yields `undefined` identically. The
  record path validates the whole bag first, so the diagnostic is deterministic;
  the array path guards as visited, so the hot path pays no second pass.

### Error matching

```ts
matchType(error, arms)            // one arm per variant; a missing arm is a COMPILE ERROR
matchType(error, arms, fallback)  // partial arms; fallback sees only the RESIDUAL variants
```

### Formatters

Presentation over the `TypedError[]` that `combineWithAllErrors` accumulates
*from an array input*. Its record form accumulates `KeyedError`s, which reach
these by `errors.map((e) => e.error)`.

```ts
groupByType(errors)    // -> a PARTIAL record keyed by `type`; groups keep their narrowed variant
prettifyErrors(errors) // -> one "✖ <type>: <message>" line per error
```

`groupByType`'s keys are optional because a variant that did not occur has no key
— typing an absent group as present would hand you `undefined` under a type that
promised an array.

`prettifyErrors` reads `type` and `message` **only**, never `details`. An empty
input gives an empty string rather than a placeholder, so it composes into a
larger message. It is **not** a redaction mechanism: a variant whose message is
computed from its payload has already put that data in `message`.

### Interop — the ways into the `Result` world

```ts
fromNullable(value, error)        // null/undefined becomes an Err
fromPredicate(value, pred, error) // narrows T when pred is a type guard
fromThrowable(fn, onThrow)        // wrap a throwing function into a Result-returning one
fromPromise(promise, onReject)    // catch a REJECTION into the error channel
fromThrowableAsync(fn, onReject)  // the lazy, reusable form of fromPromise
fromSchema(schema, options?)      // any Standard Schema validator -> a Result-returning fn
fromSchemaAsync(schema, options?) // the same, for asynchronous validation
```

### Do-notation

```ts
safeTry(function* () { … })       // drive a generator; any Err short-circuits the block
safeUnwrap(r)                     // make a plain Result yield*-able. ROOT ONLY.
```

### Test assertions

```ts
expectOk(r)   // returns T — asserts the branch, then EXTRACTS the value
expectErr(r)  // returns E — asserts the branch, then EXTRACTS the error
```

These live on the **root barrel** and need no test runner. They are not the
`/testing` matchers — see §11 for the distinction.

### Types

`Result` `Ok` `Err` `TypedError` `ErrorCtor` `ErrorsOf` `OkTypeOf` `ErrTypeOf`
`ValidationIssue` `ValidationFailed` `FromSchemaOptions` `MalformedResult`
`MalformedResultReason` `KeyedError`

---

## 4. Typed errors

`E` is **fully generic**. A `Result`'s error may be a string, a real `Error`, or
anything else. `TypedError` is an **opt-in** convention for errors you want to
narrow on:

```ts
{ type: string; message: string; details?: TData; cause?: unknown }
```

Plain objects. **Never classes. Never `extends Error`.** They serialize, and they
narrow.

- **`type`** — the stable string discriminant you switch on. Not a Node-style
  error `code`, and not `_tag`.
- **`message`** — human-readable. Keep secrets out of it; no formatter can take
  them back out.
- **`details`** — the optional, variant-typed payload. Nested under one key,
  **never spread onto the error object** — that would break the four-field shape.
- **`cause`** — `unknown`. The one non-serializable route. Strip at boundaries.

### Building them

```ts
import { defineError, defineErrors, err } from '@zireal/result-kit';
import type { ErrorsOf } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const notFound = defineError('not_found', (d: { id: string }) => `No user ${d.id}`);
const forbidden = defineError('forbidden', 'Not permitted');

// Manual union — always supported
// type AppError = ReturnType<typeof notFound> | ReturnType<typeof forbidden>;

// Registry form — one named home for the set. Pick ONE of these two; declaring
// both in the same scope is a duplicate identifier.
export const appErrors = defineErrors({ notFound, forbidden });
export type AppError = ErrorsOf<typeof appErrors>;
//          ^? TypedError<'not_found', { id: string }> | TypedError<'forbidden', never>

const failure = err(notFound({ id: 'u1' }));
//    ^? Err<TypedError<'not_found', { id: string }>>
```

`defineError`'s second argument is either a **string** (a fixed message) or a
**function** of the payload (a computed one). The constructor decides which by
counting the message function's declared parameters, which leaves exactly one
shape it cannot infer — a payload paired with a **static** message. Getting that
wrong fails *silently*:

```ts
// ✗ TYPECHECKS, then drops `details` at runtime. Nothing is declared for the
//   constructor to read, so it builds a no-payload variant.
defineError<'conflict', { id: string }>('conflict', 'Already exists');

// ✓ The escape hatch — supplies the payload type without repeating the tag.
defineError.withData<{ id: string }>()('conflict', 'Already exists');
```

Reach for `.withData` **only** for that case; the single-call form covers every
computed message.

`defineErrors` returns the object unchanged — its only job is to type-check the
bag, so a non-constructor entry is caught where you write it rather than later.

Each constructor also carries:

- `.type` — the tag, readable without building a value.
- `.is()` — a runtime guard for narrowing a union.

### Narrowing them

```ts
switch (error.type) {
  case 'not_found': return error.details?.id;
  case 'forbidden': return null;
}
```

`switch` works and narrows. `matchType` (§5) is the expression form, and adds
compile-time exhaustiveness.

---

## 5. Dispatching on the error — `matchType`

`switch (error.type)` narrows, but it is a *statement*, and it is not
exhaustive-checked without a `never` helper in the default branch. `matchType` is
the expression form, and exhaustiveness **is** the type:

```ts
import { matchType } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const status = matchType(error, {
  not_found: () => 404,
  forbidden: () => 403,
  conflict: (e) => (e.details!.slug ? 409 : 400),
});
//    ^? number — the union of every arm's return type
```

- Each arm receives its **own** narrowed variant, with its own payload.
  `conflict`'s `e.details` is `{ slug: string } | undefined`; reaching for
  `e.details!.id` there is an error.
- A **missing** arm is a compile error.
- An arm keyed on a tag the union does not have is **also** a compile error — a
  typo'd tag cannot compile as a dead arm.
- Add a variant to the union later and every `matchType` over it lights up.

### The fallback is the third parameter

```ts
const status = matchType(error, { not_found: () => 404 }, (e) => {
  //                                                       ^? forbidden | conflict
  logUnexpected(e);
  return 500;
});
```

**Never a `_` key inside the arm bag.** Only the third position can be narrowed
to the *residual* variants — the ones you did not handle. A `_` sharing the
object collapses to `never` and would hand you back the variants you just
handled. That residual narrowing is the entire reason to prefer `matchType` over
`switch`.

It is not a `default:` branch and does not see the whole union. Do not call it
"the default arm".

### Composing with `match`

`matchType` operates on the **error**, not on the `Result`. The idiomatic pairing:

```ts
const status = match(result, {
  ok: () => 200,
  err: (e) => matchType(e, { not_found: () => 404, forbidden: () => 403 }),
});
```

One leaves the `Result`; the other dispatches on the error inside it.

### Two constraints

- **`details` stays optional after the tag narrows.** Narrowing does not make the
  payload non-optional. Arms read `e.details!.id` or `e.details?.id`. That is a
  `TypedError` fact, not a `matchType` one.
- **Only a closed union can be exhausted.** A bare `TypedError` has an open
  `string` tag, so *any* set of arms satisfies it. Exhaustiveness needs a union of
  specific variants — what `ErrorsOf` or `ReturnType<typeof …> | …` gives you.

---

## 6. The two surfaces

Both are first-class and fully supported. Pick per project, or mix per file.

| | `@zireal/result-kit/fluent` | `@zireal/result-kit` |
|---|---|---|
| Style | chained methods | free functions |
| Reads like | `ok(x).map(f).unwrapOr(0)` | `unwrapOr(map(ok(x), f), 0)` |
| Best for | application code, linear pipelines | libraries, hot paths, minimal bundles |
| Bundle cost | the wrapper class | only the functions you import |

**Default to `/fluent` for application code.** Reach for the core when bundle size
matters, or when writing a library and you would rather not impose a wrapper on
your callers.

The core is **self-sufficient** — it never needs `/fluent`. That is the point of
the split, and it is something a class-based library structurally cannot offer,
because there the methods and the data are the same object.

```ts
// core — reads inside-out
import { map, mapErr, unwrapOr } from '@zireal/result-kit';
const named = map(findUser('u1'), (user) => user.name);
const label = unwrapOr(mapErr(named, (e) => e.message), 'anonymous');

// /fluent — reads left-to-right
import { from } from '@zireal/result-kit/fluent';
const label = from(findUser('u1'))
  .map((user) => user.name)
  .mapErr((e) => e.message)
  .unwrapOr('anonymous');
```

### The wrapper is transient

**The plain union is the source of truth.** A `ResultChain` is an ergonomic
envelope for the duration of one chain — never the interchange type, never the
stored type, never the serialized type.

- `from(result)` lifts a plain `Result` in.
- `.toResult()` takes you back out.
- Only the plain union carries the JSON round-trip guarantee.

`ResultChain` delegates one-to-one to the core free functions. It never
reimplements them.

### `/fluent`'s exports

`ok` `err` `from` `safeTry` `fromPromise` `fromThrowableAsync` `ResultAsync`,
plus the `ResultChain` type.

`ok` / `err` / `safeTry` / `fromPromise` / `fromThrowableAsync` exist at **both**
entrypoints under the same names — the root's return plain data, these return
wrappers. Deliberate: you should not have to learn two vocabularies.

**`ResultChain<T, E>` mirrors the core:** `.map()` `.mapErr()` `.andThen()`
`.orElse()` `.inspect()` `.inspectErr()` `.match()` `.unwrapOr()`
`.unwrapOrElse()` `.unwrapOrThrow()` `.toNullable()` `.isOk()` `.isErr()`
`.toResult()` `.toAsync()`. It also carries `.toJSON()` (which serializes the
wrapped `Result` — but exit with `.toResult()` rather than relying on it) and
`[Symbol.iterator]`, which is what makes it `yield*`-able inside `safeTry`.

### Array-shaped helpers stay root-only

`combine`, `combineWithAllErrors`, `partition`, and the three sync constructors
`fromNullable` / `fromPredicate` / `fromThrowable`. They take arrays or
non-`Result` inputs, so there is no single instance for a method to hang off.
Re-enter with `from(...)`:

```ts
from(combine([a, b])).map(sum).unwrapOr(0);
```

---

## 7. Async

### In the core

Async is just `Promise<Result<T, E>>`. **There is no new type**, and no
`Async`-suffixed twin of anything — the transforms take a value or a promise in
the same signature:

```ts
const upper = await map(loadUser(id), (user) => user.name.toUpperCase());
```

### On `/fluent`

```ts
import { ResultAsync } from '@zireal/result-kit/fluent';

const name = await ResultAsync.from(loadUser(id))
  .andThen(requireActive)
  .map((user) => user.name)
  .match({ ok: (n) => n, err: () => 'anonymous' });
```

`ResultAsync` **is `ResultChain` lifted**: every value-terminal mirrored with a
`Promise`-returning one. Terminal *handlers* stay synchronous; only the return is
lifted.

It `implements PromiseLike<Result<T, E>>`, so `await resultAsync` collapses to the
plain `Result` — by design rather than by accident. Awaiting *is* the sanctioned
way out. It also means a floating un-`await`ed chain is caught by the standard
`no-floating-promises` lint rule, for free.

**Two deliberate departures from `ResultChain`:**

1. **No `.isOk()` / `.isErr()`.** An always-truthy `if (ra.isOk())` is a footgun,
   and narrowing needs the plain union anyway.
2. **`.toJSON()` throws**, rather than silently serializing `{}` for a value that
   has not arrived yet.

### Reaching async is always explicit

Three ways in — `.toAsync()`, `fromPromise`, `ResultAsync.from` — and never
implicitly:

```ts
import { ok } from '@zireal/result-kit/fluent';   // the WRAPPER ok, not the root's

ok(user).map(validate).toAsync().andThen(saveRemote).match({
  ok: (saved) => saved.id,
  err: (e) => e.message,
});
```

**Why explicit:** a settled `Result` cannot promise an asynchronous output. A
transform may short-circuit *without calling its callback at all* — so on the
`Err` branch there would be nothing to await.

The precise consequence, which splits three ways rather than one:

- On **`ResultAsync`**, `.map()` / `.mapErr()` / `.andThen()` / `.orElse()`
  explicitly **do** accept promise-returning callbacks. You are already async.
- On a **sync** chain, `.andThen()` / `.orElse()` **reject** an async callback
  outright — their callback is typed `(value: T) => Result<U, F>`, so a
  `Promise<Result>` matches no overload. That is a loud compile error, which is
  the good case.
- On a **sync** chain, `.map()` / `.mapErr()` / `.inspect()` / `.inspectErr()`
  cannot reject it, because their callback returns an arbitrary `U`. So the
  return is typed *honestly* instead: it widens to `ResultChain | ResultAsync`
  (`Result | Promise<Result>` in the core), since which one you get depends on a
  branch taken at runtime.

Either way the fix is the same: reach for `.toAsync()` first, and the type stays
a single thing.

---

## 8. Do-notation — `safeTry`

For flows where chaining gets awkward: branches, early exits, or a step needing a
value from two steps back. The body reads as flat, sequential code, and any `Err`
short-circuits the whole block.

```ts
import { ok, safeTry, safeUnwrap } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const total = safeTry(function* () {
  const user = yield* safeUnwrap(findUser(id));      // an Err here short-circuits
  const order = yield* safeUnwrap(loadOrder(user));  // each binds its own type

  return ok(user.credit + order.total);              // return a Result EXPLICITLY
});
//    ^? Result<number, NotFound | OrderMissing>
```

The error channel is **union-accumulated** — the same rule `andThen` uses, because
do-notation *is* `andThen` chaining with nicer syntax. There is no Rust-style
`From` coercion.

**Rules for the body:**

1. **Return a `Result`, never a bare value.** `return ok(v)`, or an early
   `return err(e)`.
2. `safeUnwrap` is a **free function**, and it only ever appears inside a
   `safeTry` block.

### Async

The same overloaded runner covers both worlds — a `function*` returns the sync
shape, an `async function*` the async one. **There is no `safeTryAsync`.** Inside
an `async function*`, a `Promise<Result>` unwraps with no `await`:

```ts
const total = await safeTry(async function* () {
  const user = yield* safeUnwrap(fetchUser(id));

  return ok(user.credit);
});
```

### On `/fluent`

There is **no `safeUnwrap`** — the wrappers are self-iterable, so `yield*` them
directly, and the block hands back a wrapper so the chain continues:

```ts
import { ok, safeTry, from } from '@zireal/result-kit/fluent';

const total = safeTry(function* () {
  const user = yield* from(findUser(id));

  return ok(user.credit);
}).unwrapOr(0);
```

The root's `safeUnwrap` still works inside a fluent block, for unwrapping a
*plain* union.

**Why iterability lives on the adapter and not the union:** putting
`[Symbol.iterator]` on what `ok()` / `err()` produce would reopen the no-brand
guarantee, and with it the JSON round-trip, for the sake of optional sugar.
`ok(1)` is not iterable, and that is enforced by test.

---

## 9. Across the wire

Most error-handling libraries stop at the process boundary. This package's central
claim is that it does not.

A `Result` is plain data by contract, so it crosses intact and **stays a
`Result`** on the other side. That turns the usual boundary ceremony — a status
code, a bespoke `{ error: string }` envelope, a `try`/`catch` that flattens every
failure to a message — into nothing at all: you return the value you already had.

```ts
// server
return err(seatTaken({ seatId }));

// client — the same union, narrowed
if (isErr(result)) matchType(result.error, { seat_taken: …, flight_closed: … });
```

**End-to-end typed errors, server to client, with no codegen step.** No generated
client, no schema-to-type pipeline, no drift: the client's types are the server's
types because they are the same declarations.

### One pattern, two transports

The pattern is always *return a `Result`, narrow it on the far side*. What differs
is whether the **type** made the trip with the value.

**Transport 1 — the type crosses too** (a Next.js server action, a typed RPC
client, tRPC, a typed worker channel). Nothing to do:

```ts
const result = await bookSeat(input);

return isOk(result) ? `Booked ${result.value.seatId}` : explain(result.error);
```

Keep the framework-facing function **thin**. The action is a wrapper; the
substance is an ordinary `Result`-returning function it calls:

```ts
'use server';

export async function bookSeatAction(input: unknown) {
  return createBooking(input);   // plain TypeScript, no framework in sight
}
```

That is not tidiness. It is what keeps the pattern true on a route handler, a
queue consumer and a test without rewriting it, and it keeps your error logic out
of the one file the framework owns.

> A server action's return type is a *compiler* promise, not a runtime check.
> Across a version skew it can be wrong. `parseResult` is available there too if
> you want the belt as well as the braces — it is simply not the common case.

**Transport 2 — the type is lost** (`fetch`, `postMessage`, a message queue).
`response.json()` hands you `unknown`, and closing that gap with
`as Result<T, E>` is an assertion nothing verifies on data you did not author.
Prove it back instead, in **two steps**:

```ts
const envelope = parseResult(await response.json());
if (isErr(envelope)) return `Bad response (${envelope.error.details?.reason})`;

const result = envelope.value;                 // Result<unknown, unknown> — envelope proven
if (isErr(result)) return renderError(result.error);

const booking = parseBooking(result.value);    // fromSchema — payload proven
```

`parseResult` proves the **envelope**; `fromSchema` proves the **payload**. They
are separate steps on purpose: the envelope is provable and its cargo is not.

### `parseResult` and `isResult`

```ts
const parsed = parseResult(await response.json());

if (isErr(parsed)) {
  console.error(parsed.error.details?.reason); // see the five reasons below
  return;
}

const result = parsed.value;                  // Result<unknown, unknown>
if (isOk(result)) result.value;
```

**The nesting is deliberate.** The outer `Result` answers *was this a `Result` at
all*; the inner one *did the operation succeed*. Collapsing them would make a
corrupt envelope indistinguishable from a reported failure — the exact
distinction the function exists to draw.

Reach for `isResult` instead when you just want an `if`: it is the same check as
a type predicate, with no diagnostic and no nesting.

`MalformedResultReason` is a **closed union of five**, and branching on it is the
whole point of the type:

| Reason | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `'not_an_object'` | A primitive, `null`, or an array. |
| `'unreadable'` | An object whose own properties could not be read — a hostile `Proxy`. |
| `'missing_discriminant'` | No `ok` property at all. |
| `'invalid_discriminant'` | An `ok` property that is not a boolean. |
| `'error_dropped'` | `ok: false` with no `error` key. |

**`parseResult` is deliberately not generic.** `parseResult<User, E>(json)` would
be the same unchecked assertion wearing a friendlier face — it proves the
envelope and nothing about what it carries. Narrow the payload with `fromSchema`
or your own guard. Writing the generic form does not compile.

**It validates and never rewrites.** On success you get back *the same object*,
extra properties and all — a `traceId` your gateway stamped onto the envelope
rides through untouched. The two-field rule governs what this package *builds*,
not what it will look at.

Two rejections worth knowing, both about properties `JSON.stringify` drops:

- A round-tripped `ok()` is `{ ok: true }` with no `value` key, and it is
  **accepted** — it is the output of the form this package recommends for a void
  success.
- A bare `{ ok: false }` is **rejected**, reason `'error_dropped'`. `err` has no
  no-arg form, so that shape only arises when a payload that is not
  JSON-serializable was dropped in transit. Send `"error": null` for a failure
  with no detail. Accepting it would hand you an `Err` whose `.error` is
  `undefined`, which crashes `matchType`, `groupByType` and `prettifyErrors` one
  hop later.

### The three things that do not survive

- **`cause` may hold anything.** The one field typed `unknown`, so the one route
  a non-serializable value takes into an otherwise JSON-safe `Result`. This
  collides head-on with `fromSchema`'s `{ includeCause: true }`, which puts the
  **raw vendor issues** there — the rejected input included, so a cycle, a
  `BigInt` or a user's password can ride out in the response body. Strip `cause`
  at the boundary, in the one function that serializes. This package never
  mutates your error data to do it for you.
- **`ok()` with no argument.** Arrives as `{ ok: true }` with the `value` key
  *gone*, not `undefined`. Reading `revived.value` on that object still gives
  `undefined` and is usually fine; `'value' in revived` will surprise you. (This
  is about the round-tripped object itself — not about `parseResult`'s envelope,
  whose `.value` is the inner `Result` and is always present.)
- **The fluent wrapper.** Exit it first — serialize `chain.toResult()`.

---

## 10. Validation — `fromSchema`

Zod 4, Valibot, ArkType and Effect Schema all implement
[Standard Schema v1](https://standardschema.dev), a **types-only** spec. So one
adapter covers all of them, and the zero-dependency stance is untouched — there is
no dependency to add.

```ts
import { fromSchema, isErr } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const parseUser = fromSchema(UserSchema);   // one wrap, many calls

const result = parseUser(await req.json()); // Result<User, ValidationFailed>
if (isErr(result)) {
  for (const { path, message } of result.error.details?.issues ?? []) {
    console.log(path.join('.'), message);   // "email", "invalid email"
  }
}
```

Note `details?.issues` — `details` is optional on **every** `TypedError`, so the
`?.` is required.

The error is a **single** `TypedError<'validation_failed', { issues }>` — one
error channel, one error — so it composes with `matchType`, `groupByType` and
`combineWithAllErrors` like every other typed error. It is deliberately *not* an
array of errors: a `TypedError[]` in `E` would make `matchType` / `isTypedError` /
`unwrapOrThrow` special-case an array, and would collide with `combine`'s own
`Result<T[], E[]>`.

### What each issue keeps

Only the two fields Standard Schema *guarantees*:

- **`message`** — the vendor's own text, **passed through untouched**.
- **`path`** — normalized to `readonly (string | number)[]`. `[]` means the root.

Vendor extras — Zod's `code`, `expected`, `input` — are **dropped**. That keeps
`details` identical across vendors and provably JSON-safe, which is what lets a
validation error cross the wire under the round-trip guarantee.

**The accepted price: you cannot branch on *what kind* of failure occurred** from
`details`. Pass `{ includeCause: true }` to keep the raw issues on `cause` for
debugging. It is **off by default** because Zod attaches the rejected input, and
an always-on `cause` would retain that payload inside a value people log by
reflex.

Two things to know before logging an issue list:

- `issue.message` is the **vendor's** text and some vendors embed the rejected
  value in it — Valibot's reads `Invalid email: Received "..."`. The
  `error.message` this package authors is a **count and nothing else**, precisely
  so the one field it controls cannot carry payload. The per-issue messages are
  not under that promise.
- An empty `issues` array is still an `Err`.

### Sync vs async

`fromSchema` is synchronous and **throws** if handed an async schema — the spec's
own type says any schema *may* be async, so it cannot be caught at compile time.
`fromSchemaAsync` accepts both, and is the one to reach for when you do not know
statically which you have.

They are a **pair, not one union-returning function**: the spec types `validate`
as `Result | Promise<Result>` unconditionally, so a conditional return type would
never reduce and every caller would pay an `await` for synchronous validation.

---

## 11. Testing

A `Result` is plain data — never a class, never `extends Error` — so you assert on
it structurally, with no custom matcher and no fighting `instanceof`:

```ts
expect(await changePlan(input)).toEqual(ok({ kind: 'noop' }));
expect(await changePlan(bad)).toEqual(err(missingBaseItem()));
```

### Reading the value — `expectOk` / `expectErr`

On the **root barrel**. They need no test runner. They assert the branch, then **return** the payload —
`expectOk` gives you `T`, `expectErr` gives you `E`:

```ts
import { expectOk, expectErr } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const value = expectOk(await loadPlan(id));
expect(value.items).toHaveLength(2);

const error = expectErr(await failingCall());
expect(error.type).toBe('not_found');
```

On the wrong branch they throw a descriptive error. A `TypedError` payload (or the
`combineWithAllErrors` array of them) is rendered as a `✖ type: message` block
with `details` and `cause` beneath, rather than one line of JSON.

### Vitest matchers — `@zireal/result-kit/testing`

An **optional** subpath. `vitest` is an optional peer dependency: never installed
on your behalf, and nothing in your production bundle references it.

**Register explicitly** — importing does *not* register them, because
`sideEffects: false` would let a bundler drop an auto-registering import and leave
the matchers silently absent:

```ts
// vitest.setup.ts
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { resultMatchers } from '@zireal/result-kit/testing';

expect.extend(resultMatchers);
```

Then:

```ts
expect(await loadPlan(id)).toBeOk();
expect(await loadPlan(id)).toBeOkWith({ kind: 'noop' });

expect(await loadPlan(bad)).toBeErr();
expect(await loadPlan(bad)).toBeErrWith(missingBaseItem());

// partial matching is vitest's own, not a separate matcher
expect(await loadPlan(bad)).toBeErrWith(
  expect.objectContaining({ type: 'missing_base_item' }),
);
```

Four matchers, symmetric: `toBeOk` / `toBeOkWith` / `toBeErr` / `toBeErrWith`.
Both `*With` forms are **deep equality**; partial matching is Vitest's own
`expect.objectContaining`, which they honour. There is no `toBeErrMatching`.

**The matchers assert; they do not narrow**, because a Vitest matcher cannot say
anything about its subject's type. Keep `expectOk` / `expectErr` for reading the
value afterwards. Every failure message is delegated to those two, so the wording
is one thing with two call shapes.

---

## 12. Recipes

### Adopting `Result` in a codebase that throws

You do not have to convert everything at once. `unwrapOrThrow` is the **boundary
adapter** for a strangler migration:

```ts
import { unwrapOrThrow } from '@zireal/result-kit';

// Newly converted — returns a Result.
async function changePlan(input: Input): Promise<Result<PlanChange, BillingError>> { … }

// A throwing wrapper for callers not yet converted. One line, one leaf.
async function changePlanOrThrow(input: Input): Promise<PlanChange> {
  return unwrapOrThrow(await changePlan(input));
}
```

On `Err` it throws a real `Error` carrying the original in `cause`, so nothing is
lost. Point still-throwing callers at the `…OrThrow` wrapper and converted callers
at the `Result`-returning function; delete the wrapper when the last throwing
caller is gone.

Going the other way — wrapping a throwing dependency *into* a `Result` — use
`fromThrowable` / `fromPromise`.

### Mapping a `Result` to an HTTP response

The core takes no opinion on your framework. Map at the boundary with a small
function you own. **Do not put a `status` field on the `TypedError`** — that
breaks the four-field shape and its round-trip contract. Dispatch on the
discriminant instead:

```ts
import { isErr, matchType } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const errToStatus = (error: BillingError): number =>
  matchType(error, {
    plan_not_found: () => 404,
    missing_company_id: () => 422,
    missing_base_item: () => 409,
  });

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const result = await changePlan(await req.json());

  if (isErr(result)) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: result.error.message, type: result.error.type },
      { status: errToStatus(result.error) },
    );
  }

  return Response.json(result.value);
}
```

`matchType` is exhaustive by construction, which is the point: add a variant and
this mapping stops compiling until you give it a status. A `switch` with
`default: return 400` looks tidier and quietly maps every new error to `400`
forever.

If a status is genuinely *intrinsic* to an error rather than a presentation
choice, carry it as `details.status` — inside the payload, not at the top level.

### Presenting accumulated errors

```ts
import { combineWithAllErrors, groupByType, prettifyErrors } from '@zireal/result-kit';

const combined = combineWithAllErrors([checkName(i), checkAge(i), checkEmail(i)]);

if (!combined.ok) {
  console.error(prettifyErrors(combined.error));
  // ✖ too_short: Name must be at least 2 characters
  // ✖ out_of_range: Age must be between 13 and 120

  const groups = groupByType(combined.error);
  groups.too_short?.forEach((e) => highlight(e.details?.field));
  //     ^? TooShort[] | undefined — optional, because a variant may not have occurred
}
```

### Acquiring and releasing resources

A `safeTry` body that short-circuits **does** run its `finally` blocks — `safeTry`
closes the suspended generator rather than abandoning it, and on an
`async function*` the caller's promise waits for the full unwind.

**Reach for `using` first.** It works inside `safeTry` bodies, because the
language lowers it to the same `try/finally` the close already drives:

```ts
safeTry(function* () {
  using a = yield* safeUnwrap(openFile('a.txt'));
  using b = yield* safeUnwrap(openFile('b.txt'));
  return ok(yield* safeUnwrap(merge(a, b)));
});
```

LIFO release with zero nesting; `await using` works in an `async function*`; and
partial acquire is structurally safe — if `b`'s `yield*` short-circuits, `b` was
never bound, so only `a` is released. Requires a declaration of `Symbol.dispose`:
`lib: ES2023` does **not** provide one, so you need `@types/node` (which backfills
it) or `esnext.disposable` in `lib`.

The mistake `using` makes unwritable is the hoisted handle — `let a, b` with one
`try` and `b?.release(); a?.release()` in the `finally`. It releases a resource
that was never acquired, with no type error and no runtime error.

**When release itself can fail**, write the `finally` by hand — `Symbol.dispose`
returns `void` and cannot `yield*`:

```ts
try { return ok(yield* safeUnwrap(query(conn))); }
finally { yield* safeUnwrap(conn.close()); }
```

Know which path reports it. A cleanup `Err` is **reported on the success path**
(`return ok(v)` enters the `finally`, whose yield is the first short-circuit
`safeTry` sees, so it becomes the answer and the `ok` is dropped) and **swallowed
on the failure path** (the body's own `Err` got there first). One rule — first
`Err` wins — not two; on the failure path the original error is the one worth
keeping. Log inside the `finally` if a failed close must leave a trace.

**When the resource must outlive the block**, `try/finally` and `using` are both
lexical, so an acquiring helper cannot register its own release. The expressible
answer is inversion of control — `withConnection(use)`, a helper that owns the
block and takes your work as a callback. It costs flatness (the caller re-enters
`safeTry` at that seam) and it enforces nothing: encoding the obligation in the
type needs a requirements channel this package deliberately does not have.

### There is no `pipe`

v1's `pipe` / `pipeAsync` were removed and have no direct replacement. It is a
per-site design call between two options:

- **`/fluent`**, for a linear chain: `from(x).map(f).andThen(g)`.
- **`safeTry`**, when the steps are not a straight line.

---

## 13. Gotchas, in full

**1. A discriminated-union return widens inside `safeTry`.**

```ts
return ok({ kind: 'noop' });                    // ✗ 'noop' widens to string
return ok({ kind: 'noop' } satisfies MyUnion);  // ✓ recommended default
return ok({ kind: 'noop' } as const);           // ✓ terse; flat unions only
return ok<MyUnion>({ kind: 'noop' });           // ✓ explicit type argument
```

The generator's return type is inferred *before* it is checked against your union.

**2. `details` is optional on every `TypedError`.** Reading `error.details.issues`
does not compile; it is `error.details?.issues`. Narrowing the `type` does not
change this. Inside a `matchType` arm, `e.details!.id` is the idiom.

**3. Only a closed union can be exhausted.** A bare `TypedError` has an open
`string` tag, so any set of arms satisfies it.

**4. `ok()` with no argument round-trips to a one-field object.**
`{ ok: true, value: undefined }` serializes to `{ ok: true }` — the `value` key is
**gone**, not `undefined`. `parseResult` accepts it deliberately.

**5. A bare `{ ok: false }` is rejected by `parseResult`**, unlike its `ok`
counterpart. The asymmetry is not taste: `err` has no no-arg overload, so that
shape only ever means a non-serializable error went onto the wire.

**6. `cause` is the one field that breaks serialization.** Strip it at the
boundary. Watch for `fromSchema`'s `{ includeCause: true }` in particular.

**7. `unwrapOrThrow` is the migration's only *silent* breakage.** Coming from
1.x's `/nest` adapter, it now throws a plain `Error`, not an `HttpException` —
so under Nest's default filter a handled `404` becomes an unhandled `500`.
Nothing fails to compile; the behaviour changed underneath you. Grep for
`unwrapOrThrow` before you finish.

**8. `/fluent`'s `.isOk()` does not narrow.** See §1.

**9. An `async` callback on a *sync* chain.** `.andThen()` / `.orElse()` reject
it outright — a loud compile error. `.map()` / `.mapErr()` / `.inspect()` /
`.inspectErr()` cannot, so they widen the return to `ResultChain | ResultAsync`
(core: `Result | Promise<Result>`). Call `.toAsync()` first and the type stays a
single thing. On `ResultAsync`, promise-returning callbacks are fully supported.

**10. ESM only.** No CJS build. `moduleResolution` must be `"bundler"`,
`"node16"`, or `"nodenext"`. On CommonJS, `require('@zireal/result-kit')` works on
Node 22.12+, or use `await import(...)`.

**11. There is no `/core`, `/fp-ts`, or `/nest` entrypoint.** Those were v1 and
are gone. The root *is* the core.

**12. `combine` is tuple-preserving.** `combine([ok(1), ok('a')])` is
`Result<[number, string], never>`, not `Result<(number | string)[], never>`.

**13. `andThen` widens the error channel** to `E | F`. If you annotated an
intermediate binding with a single error type, widen the annotation.

---

## 14. Migrating from 1.x

The `ResultKit` static namespace object is **gone**. Every method is now a free
function imported from the root.

**Types**

| v1 | 5.x |
|---|---|
| `Success<T>` | `Ok<T>` (shape unchanged) |
| `Failure<E>` | `Err<E>` (shape unchanged) |
| `Result<T, E>` | **unchanged** |
| `TypedError<TType>` | `TypedError<TType, TData>` — gained an optional payload parameter |
| `TypedErrorOf<TType>` | **cut** — use `TypedError<TType>` |
| `TypedErrorUnion<TType>` | **cut** — build it from `defineError` constructors, or `ErrorsOf` |

**Constructors and guards**

| v1 | 5.x |
|---|---|
| `ResultKit.success(v)` | `ok(v)` |
| `ResultKit.failure(e)` | `err(e)` |
| `ResultKit.fail(typedError)` | `err(typedError)` — no separate typed constructor |
| `ResultKit.isSuccess(r)` | `isOk(r)` |
| `ResultKit.isFailure(r)` | `isErr(r)` |
| `ResultKit.isTypedError(e)` | `isTypedError(e)` |

**Transforms and terminals** — mostly just unnesting from `ResultKit.`, with three
exceptions:

| v1 | 5.x | |
|---|---|---|
| `ResultKit.mapError` | `mapErr` | **renamed**, not just unnested |
| `ResultKit.andThen` | `andThen` | **behaviour change** — now widens `E` to `E \| F` |
| `ResultKit.combine` | `combine` | **type change** — now tuple-preserving |

**`match`'s keys changed:**

```ts
ResultKit.match(result, { onSuccess: …, onFailure: … });  // v1
match(result, { ok: …, err: … });                          // 5.x
```

> **Find-and-replace hazard.** `onSuccess` / `onFailure` were **also** the keys of
> v1's `tap`, where they were optional. A blind `onSuccess` → `ok` replace will
> corrupt those call sites. `tap` became `inspect` / `inspectErr`, which take a
> bare function. Migrate `tap` first, then rename `match`'s keys.

**Removed entrypoints:** `/core` → the root. `/fp-ts` → convert at your own
boundary. `/nest` → map to HTTP yourself (see §12).

**The one silent breakage:** `unwrapOrThrow`. See §13, gotcha 7.

---

## 15. Vocabulary

Use these words; avoid the alternatives. Getting the vocabulary right is most of
getting the code right.

| Use | Not |
|---|---|
| `Result` | Either (the fp-ts framing this sheds), Outcome |
| `Ok` / `Err` | Success / Failure (v1 type names) |
| `ok` / `err` | success / failure / fail (v1 names) |
| `isOk` / `isErr` | isSuccess / isFailure |
| `TypedError` | TaggedError, AppError, DomainError (those are userland variants built *with* it) |
| `type` (the discriminant) | tag, `_tag`, kind, code |
| `details` | data, payload, meta, context |
| `defineError` | makeError, createError, errorType |
| `ResultChain` | ResultPipeline (the v1 class), Chain, Wrapper, Builder, "the fluent Result" |
| `ResultAsync` | AsyncResultPipeline, AsyncResult, FutureResult, TaskResult, ResultPromise |
| `safeTry` | gen (Effect's name), doNotation, attempt, tryCatch, safeTryAsync (no such thing) |
| `safeUnwrap` | unwrap (means "throws" across the genre — deliberately unused), bind, `$` |
| `matchType` | match (taken by the `Result` terminal), matchError, matchTag, exhaustive |
| `groupByType` | groupBy, byType, format, flatten |
| `prettifyErrors` | prettifyError (zod's, and it takes an object not an array), format, render |
| the fallback (of `matchType`) | "the default arm" — it is not a `default:` branch and does not see the whole union |

### Relationships

- A failed `Result` carries an `error` of type `E`; when the producer opts in,
  that `E` is a `TypedError`.
- `defineError` produces `TypedError` values; `err` wraps any `E` into a failed
  `Result`.
- `ResultChain` / `ResultAsync` wrap a `Result`; `.toResult()` is the way out, and
  the plain union is what crosses a boundary. `.toAsync()` is the one seam from
  sync to async.
- `safeTry` consumes what `safeUnwrap` (or a self-iterable wrapper) yields. The
  two always appear together.
- `matchType` consumes one `TypedError`; `match` consumes one `Result`. The
  idiomatic pairing is `match(r, { ok: …, err: (e) => matchType(e, …) })`.
- `combineWithAllErrors` produces the accumulated `TypedError[]` that
  `groupByType` and `prettifyErrors` consume. `partition`'s second half is equally
  valid input.
- `resultMatchers` delegates every failure message to `expectOk` / `expectErr`.
- The wrappers are **opt-in ergonomics, never a requirement**. That split is what
  makes the core tree-shakable.

---

Full documentation: <https://github.com/alifaroo-q/result-kit>
